approved_text: Let A, B be infinite sets of natural numbers whose n-th smallest elements a_n, b_n satisfy a_n/b_n → 1. If A + B contains all sufficiently large integers, must the number of representations n = a + b (a ∈ A, b ∈ B) be unbounded?
draft: Let A = {a_1 < a_2 < ...} and B = {b_1 < b_2 < ...} be infinite sets of positive integers with a_n/b_n → 1. If A+B contains every sufficiently large integer, must the number of representations n = a + b (a in A, b in B) be unbounded as n → ∞?
source_docstrings:
Let $A=\{1\leq a_1 < a_2 < \cdots\}$ and $B=\{1\leq b_1 < b_2 < \cdots\}$ be sets of integers with
$a_n/b_n\to 1$.

If $A+B$ contains all sufficiently large positive integers then is it true that
$\limsup 1_A\ast 1_B(n)=\infty$?

A conjecture of Erdős and Sárközy.
